name: Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young Type 2 (GCK-MODY)

clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous inactivating variants in GCK, which encodes glucokinase, the beta-cell glucose sensor; inheritance is autosomal dominant with near-complete penetrance.
Produces mild, stable, non-progressive fasting hyperglycaemia present from birth rather than diabetes that worsens over time.
The glucose increment during an oral glucose tolerance test is characteristically small because the defect resets the glucose set-point rather than abolishing insulin secretion.
HbA1c is typically only mildly raised and remains stable across decades, distinguishing it from progressive forms of MODY.
Most non-pregnant patients require no pharmacological treatment; diet and lifestyle suffice and drugs rarely improve the fasting level.
Microvascular and macrovascular complications are uncommon, so aggressive glucose-lowering is generally unnecessary and unhelpful.
In pregnancy, management hinges on whether the fetus has inherited the mutation: an unaffected fetus of an affected mother may overgrow and may warrant maternal treatment.
Frequently discovered incidentally on routine screening, in pregnancy, or during family testing rather than through symptomatic presentation.
reference.pathophysiology: MODY2 results from heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in GCK, the gene encoding glucokinase (hexokinase IV). Glucokinase catalyses the rate-limiting phosphorylation of glucose in the pancreatic beta cell and hepatocyte and functions as the principal glucose sensor that couples ambient glucose concentration to insulin secretion. A partial reduction in glucokinase activity raises the threshold at which glucose triggers insulin release, effectively resetting the glucostat to a higher level; the beta cell still secretes insulin appropriately, but only once a slightly higher glucose concentration is reached. The consequence is a modest, lifelong elevation of fasting glucose that is tightly regulated and does not progress, because the underlying secretory machinery and beta-cell mass are intact. Reduced hepatic glucokinase activity also blunts postprandial glycogen synthesis, contributing to the small glucose excursion after a carbohydrate load. Because regulation around the new set-point remains physiological, chronic hyperglycaemia is mild and the long-term risk of diabetic complications is low. Rare biallelic inactivating mutations instead cause permanent neonatal diabetes, while activating GCK mutations cause congenital hyperinsulinism, illustrating the gene's dose-dependent role.
additionalDifferentials: Impaired fasting glucose or early type 2 diabetes mellitus
HNF1A-MODY and HNF4A-MODY, which are progressive and treatment-responsive rather than stable
Gestational diabetes mellitus when first detected in pregnancy
Type 1 diabetes mellitus (autoantibody positive) when hyperglycaemia is mistakenly thought significant
Laboratory artefact or non-fasting sampling causing apparent hyperglycaemia
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of GCK, typically within a MODY panel
Fasting plasma glucose demonstrating mild, stable elevation
Oral glucose tolerance test showing a characteristically small glucose increment
Serial HbA1c confirming a persistently mild and stable value over time
Pancreatic autoantibodies to exclude autoimmune diabetes
Fetal growth ultrasound surveillance in affected pregnancies
Family screening of first-degree relatives with fasting glucose
redFlags: HbA1c or fasting glucose rising well beyond the expected mild range, suggesting a coexisting second cause of diabetes
Development of significant microvascular complications, which is atypical and warrants re-evaluation
Fetal macrosomia in an affected mother carrying an unaffected fetus, indicating need for maternal glucose management
Symptomatic osmotic symptoms such as marked polyuria or polydipsia, which are inconsistent with isolated GCK-MODY
reference.prognosis: Excellent: fasting hyperglycaemia is mild and stable lifelong, treatment is usually unnecessary outside pregnancy, and the risk of clinically significant diabetic complications is low. Correct genetic diagnosis spares patients unnecessary medication, monitoring and insurance implications.
pitfalls: Escalating glucose-lowering therapy in pursuit of normoglycaemia, which is ineffective and exposes patients to hypoglycaemia and side effects
Misdiagnosing the condition as type 1 or type 2 diabetes and applying inappropriate lifelong treatment
In pregnancy, treating the mother without considering fetal genotype, risking impaired fetal growth if the fetus is also affected
Assuming the mild hyperglycaemia will inevitably progress and over-monitoring the patient
Overlooking the strongly hereditary pattern and failing to test and reassure relatives
management: Recognise that most non-pregnant patients need no glucose-lowering drugs and manage with diet and lifestyle alone
Avoid unnecessary pharmacotherapy, monitoring and the diagnostic label burden once GCK-MODY is genetically confirmed
In pregnancy, guide treatment by foetal genotype, considering insulin if an unaffected foetus shows accelerated growth but withholding intensive treatment if the foetus is affected
Undertake foetal growth ultrasound surveillance in affected pregnancies
Reassure patients that microvascular and macrovascular complication risk is low and aggressive glucose-lowering is unhelpful
Provide genetic counselling and family glucose and genetic screening for autosomal dominant inheritance
